passages.t: How can a mortal be right before God?
passages.happening:
‘Then Job answered’ (verse 1). “Yes, I know that it is so, but how can a mortal be righteous before God? If one wished to contend with God, he could not answer Him one time out of a thousand” (verses 2-3).

God is wise and mighty. He moves mountains and shakes the earth, commands the sun not to shine and seals off the stars. “He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea. He is the Maker of the Bear and Orion, of the Pleiades and the constellations of the south” (verses 8-9).

“Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him; were He to move, I would not recognize Him” (verse 11). If he takes away, who can stop him? ‘God does not restrain His anger; the helpers of Rahab cower beneath Him’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Job does not deny what Bildad said about God's justice. He raises a harder problem. If God is both the one Job accuses and the judge of the case, and infinitely stronger than the man who brings it, how could the case ever be heard fairly?

The chapter is full of courtroom words. To contend, riv, is to bring a lawsuit. To be righteous, tsadaq, in a court means to be declared in the right. Disputes were settled at the city gate before the elders, and Job imagines summoning God there.

The hymn of verses 5 to 10 could stand in a psalm of praise, but here it serves a dark point: such a God cannot be faced in court. The stars of verse 9 were familiar markers in the night sky, though the Hebrew names are not certainly identified. Rahab here is not the woman of Jericho, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew. It is a poet's name for a monster of chaos, and elsewhere it can stand for Egypt (Psalm 87:4; Isaiah 30:7).
passages.later: The Psalms say the same of God's power over the sea: “Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found” (Psalm 77:19).
passages.asks: Job believed God was all-powerful, and that made his suffering harder, not easier. Ask whether you have felt that. And ask what you would say to God if you could stand before him and be heard.

passages.t: Even if he were in the right
passages.happening:
“How then can I answer Him or choose my arguments against Him? For even if I were right, I could not answer. I could only beg my Judge for mercy” (verses 14-15). If Job summoned God, he does not believe God would listen. He would be crushed in a storm, wounded ‘without cause’ (verse 17).

“If it is a matter of strength, He is indeed mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon Him?” (verse 19). Even if he were blameless, his own mouth would declare him guilty. “Though I am blameless, I have no concern for myself; I despise my own life” (verse 21).

Then he says the darkest thing yet. It is all the same, he says; God destroys both the blameless and the wicked. “When the scourge brings sudden death, He mocks the despair of the innocent. The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; He blindfolds its judges. If it is not He, then who is it?” (verses 23-24).
passages.hearers:
Job uses the word the LORD used in 2:3, without cause, chinnam. He does not know that God has said it of him. To Job, God is simply too strong to be brought to court.

Job's question in verse 2 picks up Eliphaz's question from 4:17, but turns it. Eliphaz meant that no one is morally pure before God. Job means that no one could win a case against him.

Verse 24 is important. Job will not explain his suffering by chance or by some other power. Everything is in God's hand, which makes his question sharper, not easier.
passages.later: The prophets asked the same question of God's justice: “Righteous are You, O LORD, when I plead before You. Yet about Your judgments I wish to contend with You: Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” (Jeremiah 12:1).
passages.hard:
Job says God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike, and mocks the innocent. Is the Bible saying that?

These are Job's words in the depth of his agony, not the narrator's verdict. The book lets him say them because they express how the world looks to someone in his place, and because the friends' tidy answers cannot be tested without them. The book does not endorse them as final. When God speaks, he challenges Job's charge of injustice (40:8), and Job takes back his words (42:6). Yet God also says that Job spoke more rightly than his friends (42:7). Readers have taken this to mean that Job's honesty about what he could see was nearer the truth than the friends' false confidence, even though his conclusions went too far. The book holds both the protest and the correction.

When Job says he despises his own life (verse 21), the book records his anguish honestly. It does not commend it.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job refused to blame chance. He took his complaint to the only one who could answer it. Ask where you take your hardest questions. And ask whether you let others say dark things in grief without rushing to correct them.

passages.t: No one to stand between them
passages.happening:
“My days are swifter than a runner; they flee without seeing good. They sweep by like boats of papyrus, like an eagle swooping down on its prey” (verses 25-26).

If he tried to forget his complaint and smile, he would still dread his suffering, sure that God would not acquit him. If he washed himself with snow and cleaned his hands with lye, God would plunge him into the pit, and his own clothes would despise him.

“For He is not a man like me, that I can answer Him, that we can take each other to court. Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both” (verses 32-33). If only God would take his rod away, Job could speak without fear. “But as it is, I am on my own” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
The speed of Job's days comes in three pictures: a runner, a light boat, a diving eagle.

Lye was an alkaline cleanser made from plant ash, and snow water was thought especially pure. Job says no washing would make him clean in God's court.

The mediator of verse 33 was a familiar figure: an arbiter both parties trusted, who could lay a hand on each, a sign of authority over them both, and decide between them. The word, from yakach, names one who settles a dispute. Job's despair is that no such person exists, because no one stands above God. A few Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient Greek and Syriac translations read the line as a wish, that there were a mediator between them, and some modern translations follow them.

This longing starts a thread that runs through the book. Job will speak of a witness in heaven (16:19) and of a Redeemer who lives (19:25).
passages.later: Job's light boats were known along the Nile. Isaiah speaks of a land ‘which sends couriers by sea, in papyrus vessels on the waters’ (Isaiah 18:2).
passages.asks: Job longed for someone to stand between him and God. Ask whether you have felt that distance. And ask who has stood with you, or for you, when you could not speak for yourself.
